analysis.one_liner: Ends federal tax breaks, royalty relief, and fee waivers for large oil companies and collects fees on idle federal leases.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; after referral to two committees and a subcommittee, it died there with 8 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end a long list of federal tax breaks that currently go to large oil and gas companies, including credits for enhanced oil recovery, the percentage depletion allowance, deductions for intangible drilling costs, LIFO accounting, and favorable treatment of foreign taxes. It would also charge annual fees on companies holding federal leases where no oil or gas is being produced, require companies to renegotiate old Gulf of Mexico leases so royalties are owed even when prices rise, and make offshore drillers pay for the cost of inspecting their own platforms instead of taxpayers footing the bill. The revenue would go to reducing the federal deficit and debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently help fund subsidies for companies with more than $50 million in gross receipts; future taxpayers benefit if deficits shrink, and taxpayers stop covering the cost of inspecting offshore oil facilities. Small oil producers under the $50 million threshold keep their existing tax treatment.

how_it_helps.text: Removes an enhanced oil recovery credit, percentage depletion, intangible drilling cost deductions, tertiary injectant deductions, passive-loss treatment, and the domestic production deduction for companies with more than $50 million in annual gross receipts [S2][S3].
Charges $4-$8 per acre per year (in 2011 dollars) on federal onshore and offshore leases where little or no production occurs, with proceeds deposited in the Treasury general fund [S3].

Requires holders of old Gulf of Mexico leases issued from 1996-2000, which suspend royalties when prices are low, to amend them so royalty payments apply at the price thresholds set in the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, and bars new leases or lease transfers to companies that refuse [S2][S3].

Makes offshore operators pay nonrefundable inspection fees equal to the Interior Department's annual inspection costs, deposited in an Ocean Energy Enforcement Fund used only for inspections [S2][S3].
Directs that royalties and rentals from affected leases be used for federal budget deficit reduction or, if there is no deficit, paying down the federal debt [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large oil and gas companies, which would lose multiple tax breaks, pay fees on idle federal leases and inspection fees, and renegotiate Gulf of Mexico royalty holidays. Some portion of these added costs could be passed through to consumers in energy prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves all of the same tax breaks in place for smaller oil and gas producers with $50 million or less in gross receipts, so the subsidy repeal is only partial and creates a two-tier system [S3].
Per-acre idle-lease fees of $4-$8 are small relative to lease values, so companies could find holding unused acreage cheaper than developing it, limiting the fee's incentive effect [S3].

Requiring renegotiation of existing Gulf of Mexico leases and denying new leases to companies that refuse could be contested in court and would likely face strong industry resistance, and higher compliance costs for large producers could partly show up in consumer energy prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but moderate: ending tax breaks for large oil companies, collecting royalties that current lease terms waive, and making industry pay for its own safety inspections would raise revenue and reduce deficits without raising anyone's income tax rates. The design is imperfect: the $50 million threshold exempts a large share of smaller producers, the idle-lease fees are modest, and the added costs on large producers could pass through to energy prices at least partly. On balance, the bill shifts costs from taxpayers to the most profitable energy companies, which is why industry opposition was likely to be intense.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Natural Resources and Ways and Means committees, then sent to a Natural Resources subcommittee, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on February 8, 2013, joined by Rep. Earl Blumenauer [S1][S3].

The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources and, in addition, to the Committee on Ways and Means; a month later it was referred to the Natural Resources Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
Eight Democratic cosponsors signed on during the Congress, and no Republican did [S4].
No further action was recorded through the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015: no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil and gas companies are better off because the bill died: they kept their tax credits, depletion allowances, LIFO accounting, favorable foreign tax treatment, royalty-suspension terms on old Gulf of Mexico leases, and taxpayer-funded facility inspections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large oil and gas companies kept their subsidies

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill combining tax subsidy repeal, idle-lease fees, Gulf royalty renegotiation, and offshore inspection fees.

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Joined Markey in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill during the 113th Congress.

against.name: Rep. Doc Hastings

against.role: Oil and gas industry trade association
against.what_they_did: Industry groups consistently opposed repealing oil and gas tax provisions and royalty changes of this kind during this period.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats and none of the eight later cosponsors was a Republican; the Republican-controlled committees took no action, and no roll-call votes were ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill strips an enhanced oil recovery credit, percentage depletion, intangible drilling cost deductions, tertiary injectant deductions, passive-loss treatment, the domestic production deduction, LIFO accounting, and favorable foreign tax credit rules from companies with over $50 million in gross receipts [S3]. It also ends royalty-suspension terms on old Gulf of Mexico leases, charges fees on idle federal leases, and makes operators pay for offshore safety inspections, costs that currently fall on taxpayers or are waived [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Small and midsize oil and gas producers (under $50M receipts)
industries.note: The bill's threshold exempts them from every tax provision in Title IV, so they keep the credits and deductions that large competitors lose, which preserves a taxpayer-supported advantage for them [S3].

Operators would pay inspection fees for the first time, but the fees fund the safety inspections of offshore facilities, which industry itself benefits from in avoided accidents and shutdowns after incidents like Deepwater Horizon [S2][S3].
